content: Health Reimbursement Accounts (HRAs), also known as Health Reimbursement Arrangements, are employer-funded plans that are approved by the IRS. These plans allow employers to reimburse employees for specific medical expenses that are not covered by the company’s standard health insurance plan. The reimbursable expenses may include items such as copayments, coinsurance, deductibles, and certain medical or dental services, as long as these are explicitly outlined in the HRA plan document. The rules governing HRAs are defined under IRS Section 105. For an expense to qualify for reimbursement, it must be described in the HRA plan document at the time the plan is established. Employers have the flexibility to design their HRA plans to include or exclude specific types of medical services, dental services, or cost-sharing elements like copays and deductibles. Additionally, employers can offer multiple HRA plans to accommodate different groups of employees or needs. Unlike some other health benefit accounts, employers are not required to pre-fund HRAs. Instead, they reimburse employees for eligible claims as they are submitted. For employers, these reimbursements are tax-deductible. For employees, the reimbursements are not considered taxable income, provided the expenses meet the criteria for qualified health care expenses as defined in Section 105. HRAs are established and funded solely by the employer. Employees do not contribute to these accounts or pay for the right to participate. Typically, HRAs are administered by a third-party administrator or a plan service provider. Employers may also choose to allow unused funds in an employee’s HRA account to roll over from one year to the next, similar to a savings account. The employer determines whether rollover is permitted and, if so, how much can be carried over—this could be a fixed amount or a percentage of the remaining balance. One common criticism of HRAs is the lack of transparency in their rules and requirements. Employees often find the reimbursement process confusing, and the criteria for eligible expenses can appear inconsistent or unclear. This has led to situations where employees lose access to funds they believed were available for healthcare expenses, only to discover after a procedure or test that the expense was not eligible for reimbursement. Complaints about the management of HRAs are typically addressed through channels established under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA).
